titleText.es: Ah, eh... y si pregunta el gobierno ruso, ese submarino siempre ha estado ahí.
titleText.en: Oh, and, uh, if the Russian government asks, that submarine was always there.
titleText.noteEn: The title text extends the silent submarine reveal with the official source's joke about plausible deniability.

applications.explanationEn: Espera is the positive informal command used to tell one familiar person to wait.
Patina is the positive informal command of patinar for one familiar person.

excludedUnits.rationale: AWOOGA is the unchanged English alarm sound printed in the official source, not a Spanish lexical item.

regions.labelEs: ESO QUE LLEVAS ES MI SOMBRERO.

applications.explanationEn: Eso names the thing, and que connects it to llevas, which adds the information that the other person is wearing it.

regions.labelEs: ASÍ QUE AL FINAL ME HAS ENCONTRADO.

applications.explanationEn: Así and que form the fixed connector that presents the following statement as a result or conclusion.
Al and final combine as the fixed expression for an eventual outcome.
Has is the present helper for one familiar person, and encontrado is encontrar's completed-action form.

regions.labelEs: NO ME LO HAS PUESTO FÁCIL.

applications.explanationEn: Has is the present helper for one familiar person, and puesto is poner's irregular completed-action form.
Me identifies the person affected, lo stands for the situation, and has puesto fácil describes how that situation has been made.
Neutral lo turns suficiente into an idea or amount: what is sufficient, or enough.

regions.labelEs: PORQUE SI PRETENDÍAS PERMANECER PERDIDA PARA SIEMPRE,

applications.explanationEn: Permanecer presents the state as continuing, and perdida is feminine singular because it describes the woman.
Para and siempre stay together as the fixed time expression for an unending duration.
Cometiste supplies the conventional verb, and un error names the mistake.
Me identifies the speaker as the person experiencing the liking, while gusta stays singular because mi sombrero is one liked thing.
Me identifies the speaker as the person who loses the item; quitaste is the changed past verb, and el sombrero names the thing taken away.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

example.en: Open the window.

cards.noteEn: Patina tells one familiar person to skate. It is the positive tú command of patinar.

example.en: Skate carefully.

cards.noteEn: Bruum imitates a low, sustained rumbling or roaring sound. Its repeated vowel stretches the sound on the page.

example.en: The engine went “vroom.”

cards.noteEn: Neec is a drawn-out comic sound for a heavy object or hinge creaking open.

example.en: The door creaked.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: you are wearing; you have on
cards.noteEn: Llevar often means “to carry,” but with clothes or an accessory it means to wear or have that item on. Llevas addresses one familiar person.

example.en: You are wearing a blue jacket.

cards.noteEn: Sombrero is the general Spanish word for a hat with a brim; it does not name only the Mexican style called a sombrero in English.

example.es: Dejó el sombrero junto a la puerta.
example.en: He left the hat beside the door.

cards.answerEn: so; therefore (as part of así que)

cards.questionEn: How do you connect a situation to its result with “so”?
cards.answerEn: Use así que before the result.
cards.noteEn: Así que joins a cause or situation to what follows from it. The two words work together as one connector; translating así and que separately will not give the intended meaning.

example.es: Está lloviendo, así que llevo un paraguas.
example.en: It is raining, so I am carrying an umbrella.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a result connector
in the; part of al final (“in the end”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say “in the end” or “eventually”?
cards.noteEn: Al final can name the literal end of something or the eventual outcome after events have unfolded.

example.en: In the end, we decided to stay.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.en: I have finished.

cards.answerEn: for me; marks the person something is made easy or difficult for
cards.noteEn: With ponerlo fácil or ponerlo difícil, me identifies the speaker as the person who experiences the easier or harder situation.

example.en: They do not make it easy for me.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone makes a situation easy for another person?
cards.answerEn: Use a short person word, lo, a form of poner, and fácil: me lo pones fácil, nos lo puso fácil, and so on.
cards.noteEn: The short person word identifies who benefits: me, te, le, nos, os, or les. Lo stands for the situation, poner changes for person and time, and fácil describes the resulting difficulty. With haber, use the irregular completed-action form puesto.

example.en: They made it easy for us.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes ponerlo fácil
cards.noteEn: In ponerlo fácil, lo stands for the situation being made easy. Natural English normally expresses this as “make it easy” without translating lo separately.

example.es: El profesor nos lo puso fácil.
example.en: The teacher made it easy for us.

cards.answerEn: made it easy (completed-action form in ponerlo fácil)
cards.noteEn: Puesto is poner's irregular completed-action form. With a form of haber and ponerlo fácil or difícil, it describes how someone has made a situation.

example.en: They have made it difficult for us.

cards.noteEn: The opposite is difícil, ‘difficult.’ Fácil keeps its written accent in the singular.

example.en: The exercise is easy.

cards.noteEn: Penetraste is the completed past form of penetrar for one familiar person. Penetrar en can describe entering a physical place or reaching into someone's private thoughts and feelings.

example.en: You entered the cave.

cards.answerEn: into; introduces what is entered after penetrar
cards.noteEn: Penetrar en presents a movement or reach into a place, material, subject, or person's inner world.

example.es: El agua penetró en la pared.
example.en: The water seeped into the wall.

cards.noteEn: As a noun, interior can mean the inside of something. Applied to a person, it can refer figuratively to private thoughts, feelings, or character.

example.es: Guardaba ese miedo en su interior.
example.en: She kept that fear inside herself.

cards.answerEn: the (neutral article before an adjective, as in lo mejor)
cards.noteEn: Neutral lo turns an adjective into an abstract idea: lo importante means “the important thing,” not a masculine noun.

example.en: The important thing is to begin.

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to “what is important,” “the difficult part,” or another general quality without naming a noun?
cards.answerEn: Put the unchanged word lo before a masculine-singular adjective: lo importante, lo difícil, lo bueno.
cards.noteEn: Here lo does not stand for a masculine object. It turns the quality into a general idea or aspect, such as lo importante, “what is important.” The adjective stays in its masculine singular form because there is no named noun for it to match.

example.en: The difficult part is starting.

cards.noteEn: Suficiente describes an adequate amount or degree. After neutral lo, lo suficiente means “enough” or “what is sufficient.”

example.en: That is enough.

cards.noteEn: Pretender usually means to intend, aim, or claim—not the English verb “pretend.” Pretendías presents one familiar person's intention as background in the past.

example.en: Did you intend to stay here?

cards.noteEn: Permanecer emphasizes continuing in the same place, condition, or state.

example.en: The door must remain closed.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something remains in the same state?
cards.answerEn: Use permanecer followed by a describing word that matches the person or thing.
cards.noteEn: Permanecer emphasizes that the state continues. The description changes when needed: permanecer cerrado, permanecer abierta, permanecer tranquilos.

example.en: The windows remained open.

cards.noteEn: Perdida describes a feminine person or thing that is lost. It can describe not knowing where one is or being unable to find one's way.

example.en: The hiker was still lost.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins para siempre, “forever”
cards.noteEn: Para and siempre form the fixed time expression para siempre. Here para does not introduce a purpose.

example.en: I want to live here forever.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something continues forever?
cards.answerEn: Use the fixed expression para siempre.
cards.noteEn: The two words stay together for the time meaning “forever” or “for good.” It does not use para's ordinary purpose meaning.

example.en: We will not be here forever.

cards.noteEn: Siempre alone commonly means “always.” After para, the complete expression para siempre means “forever.”

example.en: She will keep the letter forever.

cards.noteEn: Cometiste is the completed past form of cometer for one familiar person. Spanish commonly uses cometer with an error, crime, or other wrongful act.

example.en: You made a small mistake.

cards.questionEn: What verb does Spanish commonly use for making a mistake?
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses cometer with errors, mistakes, crimes, and similar wrongful acts. English says “make a mistake” but “commit an error,” so the most natural English verb depends on the noun.

example.en: We can all make a mistake.

cards.noteEn: Error can describe a mistaken action, judgment, or result. In computing it can also mean an error or bug, but this card teaches the ordinary mistake sense.

example.en: It was an honest mistake.

cards.answerEn: marks me as the person who likes something
cards.noteEn: With gustar, Spanish presents the liked thing as pleasing to a person. Me identifies the speaker as that person; it does not become a separate English word when the natural translation uses “I.”

example.en: I like coffee.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone likes one thing or several things?
cards.answerEn: Use me, te, le, nos, os, or les for the person; then use gusta for one liked thing and gustan for more than one.
cards.noteEn: Spanish builds this as if the liked thing is pleasing to the person. The liked thing controls the verb: gusta este libro but gustan estos libros. You can clarify the person with a phrase beginning with a, such as a Marta or a quien.

example.es: A Marta le gustan los gatos.
example.en: Marta likes cats.

cards.answerEn: I like; is pleasing to me
cards.noteEn: With me before it, gusta expresses that one thing or situation is pleasing to the speaker. The liked thing controls the verb: use gusta for one thing and gustan for more than one.

example.en: I like this book.

cards.answerEn: from me; marks me as the person who loses the thing
cards.noteEn: With quitar, me identifies the speaker as the person something is taken away from. Natural English often uses “from me” or a possessive such as “my.”

example.en: They took my phone away.

cards.promptEs: me/te/le/nos/os/les + quitar + cosa (+ a alguien o algo)
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone takes one thing away from another person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Use a short word such as me or le with quitar, then name the thing taken away. You can add a followed by the person or thing that is deprived of it.
cards.noteEn: Quitar changes for the person and time. The short word identifies the person or thing that loses something: me, te, le, nos, os, or les. With an unchanged dictionary-form verb, attach it as in quitarle; with a changed verb, place it before, as in le quita or me quitaste. Spanish can repeat or clarify the affected entity after a, even though English uses ‘from’ or a possessive. In the prompt, each plus sign means ‘followed by,’ and the parentheses mark the optional clarifying phrase.

example.es: Ana le quita el juguete a Luis.
example.en: Ana takes the toy away from Luis.

cards.noteEn: Quitaste is the completed past form of quitar for one familiar person. A short person word before it can identify who loses the thing.

example.en: You took the key away from him.

cards.answerEn: my here; Spanish uses el because me already marks the affected owner
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses the definite article before an owned item when a short word such as me, te, or le already identifies the affected owner. English commonly uses a possessive instead.

example.en: They broke my phone.
